coredata.dc:description: Urethanase (EC 3.5.1.75) is an effective enzyme for removing ethyl carbamate (EC) present in alcoholic beverages. However, urethanase is not well studied and has not yet been developed for practical use. In this study, we report a new urethanase (CPUTNase) from the yeast Candida parapsilosis. Because C. parapsilosis can assimilate EC as its sole nitrogen source, the enzyme was extracted from yeast cells and purified using ion-exchange chromatography. The CPUTNase was estimated as a homotetramer comprising four units of a 61.7 kDa protein. In a 20% ethanol solution, CPUTNase had 73% activity compared with a solution without ethanol. Residual activity after 18 h indicated that CPUTNase was stable in 0%–40% ethanol solutions. The optimum temperature of CPUTNase was 43°C. This enzyme showed urethanase activity at pH 5.5–10.0 and exhibited its highest activity at pH 10. The gene of CPUTNase was identified, and a recombinant enzyme was expressed in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Characteristics of recombinant CPUTNase were identical to the native enzyme. The putative amino acid sequence indicated that CPUTNase was an amidase family protein. Further, substrate specificity supported this sequence analysis because CPUTNase showed higher activities toward amide compounds. These results suggest that amidase could be a candidate for urethanase. We discovered a new enzyme and investigated its enzymatic characteristics, sequence, and recombinant CPUTNase expression. These results contribute to a further understanding of urethanase.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Urethanase (EC 3.5.1.75) is an effective enzyme for removing ethyl carbamate (EC) present in alcoholic beverages. However, urethanase is not well studied and has not yet been developed for practical use. In this study, we report a new urethanase (CPUTNase) from the yeast Candida parapsilosis. Because C. parapsilosis can assimilate EC as its sole nitrogen source, the enzyme was extracted from yeast cells and purified using ion-exchange chromatography. The CPUTNase was estimated as a homotetramer comprising four units of a 61.7 kDa protein. In a 20% ethanol solution, CPUTNase had 73% activity compared with a solution without ethanol. Residual activity after 18 h indicated that CPUTNase was stable in 0%–40% ethanol solutions. The optimum temperature of CPUTNase was 43°C. This enzyme showed urethanase activity at pH 5.5–10.0 and exhibited its highest activity at pH 10. The gene of CPUTNase was identified, and a recombinant enzyme was expressed in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Characteristics of recombinant CPUTNase were identical to the native enzyme. The putative amino acid sequence indicated that CPUTNase was an amidase family protein. Further, substrate specificity supported this sequence analysis because CPUTNase showed higher activities toward amide compounds. These results suggest that amidase could be a candidate for urethanase. We discovered a new enzyme and investigated its enzymatic characteristics, sequence, and recombinant CPUTNase expression. These results contribute to a further understanding of urethanase.

ce:sections.ce:para: Urethanase (EC 3.5.1.75) catalyzes the hydrolysis of ethyl carbamate (EC) to ethanol, carbon dioxide, and ammonia. EC is now classified as a group 2A carcinogen, but it is widely present in many foods and liquor. The EC present in sake, for example, is formed from ethanol and urea, which is the precursor of EC. Strategies to reduce the accumulation of urea in sake include the development of non-urea-producing sake yeast (1,2) and the use of acid urease (3,4). However, because other alcoholic beverages contain EC formed by other mechanisms (5,6), it has become necessary to develop alternative methods than reducing urea to remove EC directly from alcoholic beverages. However, no practical method has yet been developed to degrade EC once it has been formed in alcoholic beverages. An enzymatic strategy for reducing EC is one practical method for this; however, urethanase is not commercially available. In fact, the study of urethanase itself has been very limited. To understand urethanase and its potential application in the food and alcohol industry, we first include a brief history of our current understanding of this enzyme.

The first reported urethanase was isolated from Citrobacter sp. by Kobashi et al. (7). Gel filtration purification indicated that its activity was detected in 500–600 kDa sized fractions. Urethanases from Bacillus licheniformis and B. thiaminolyticus (8,9) were then discovered and studied, and the molecular mass of urethanase from B. licheniformis IFO12107 was 160 kDa (a homotetramer consisting of four 42 kDa proteins). Another urethanase found in Micrococcus sp. isolated from a marine sponge was identified to be a cell-associated protein. Furthermore, the crude enzyme showed 83% urethanase activity in 20% ethanol and 100% activity in 0% ethanol (10). All of these bacterial urethanases were intracellular enzymes for which protein sequences were not described. Akutsu-Shigeno et al. (11) later reported that a 55 kDa protein from the bacterium Rhodococcus equi TB-60 exhibited urethanase activity. This enzyme showed wide substrate specificity toward anilides, amides, carbamates, and esters, but activity toward EC was weak. Its sequence was registered as DD291329. The only known fungal urethanase to date was isolated from Penicillium variabile JN-A525 (12,13). Its molecular mass was determined to be 96 kDa by gel filtration; as sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS–PAGE) analysis indicated a 13.7 kDa protein, it was predicted to be a heptamer, but its amino acid sequence was not determined. Recently, ureases from some bacteria were reported to have urethanase activity (14–16). These bacterial ureases are complexes consisting of three different proteins. This kind of urease is a bifunctional enzyme having dual activity toward urea and EC, although most reported urethanases do not have activity toward urea.

Although it is possible that various types of urethanase exist, studies of urethanase are limited to those described above. Thus, obtaining a better understanding of these enzymes requires the discovery and study of other urethanases. Previously, it was shown that some yeasts were effective to degrade EC in a patent (17). However, the urethanase was not identified. We therefore preliminarily searched yeasts to degrade EC. The yeast Candida parapsilosis assimilated EC as its sole nitrogen source, and extracts from this yeast exhibited urethanase activity. In this study, we report the purification and characterization of this new urethanase from the yeast C. parapsilosis.

ce:section.ce:section-title: MATERIALS AND METHODS
Strain and media
ce:section.ce:para: C. parapsilosis NBRC 708 was obtained from the Culture Collection Division of the Biological Resource Center of the National Institute of Technology and Evaluation (NBRC). EC was purchased from Wako Pure Chemical Industries (Osaka, Japan). Urethane-containing medium consisted of 2% glycerol, 0.17% Difco Yeast nitrogen base without amino acids and ammonium sulfate (Becton, Dickinson and Company, Franklin Lakes, MD, USA), and 1% EC. YPD medium for Saccharomyces cerevisiae consisted of 2% glucose, 2% peptone, and 1% yeast extract.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Culture and extraction of crude enzyme
ce:section.ce:para: Preculture of C. parapsilosis NBRC 708 was prepared in 10 mL of urethane-containing medium within L-shaped tubes at 30°C for 7 days. It was inoculated into 500 mL of the same medium at 0.1 of initial OD660 in a 2 L baffled Erlenmeyer flask and cultured at 30°C with vigorous aeration in a shaker at 120 rpm for 8 days. Yeast cells were harvested by centrifugation, washed with cold water, and stored at −30°C. Cells were disrupted with glass beads using a Multi-beads Shocker (Yasui Kikai, Osaka, Japan) with 2500 rpm for 1800 s (a repeat of 30 s on and off) at 4°C. After 5 mL of 20 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 6.0) was added, the supernatant was transferred to a new tube for dialysis. Cell extract was dialyzed for 1 day against a 20 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 6.0) at 4°C. After centrifugation at 20,000 ×g. for 30 min, the supernatant was filtered through a membrane (pore size 0.45 μm) and used in subsequent purifications.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Measurement of ethanol and ammonia concentrations
ce:section.ce:para: The concentration of ethanol was determined using Enzytec fluid ethanol (R-Biopharm AG, Darmstadt, Germany). The concentration of ammonia was determined by an Ammonia-Test-Wako kit (Wako Pure Chemical Industries).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Urethanase activity
ce:section.ce:para: We confirmed that same molar amounts of ammonia and ethanol were produced in degradation of EC by this urethanase. Therefore, the urethanase activity was assayed by measuring the amount of NH3 produced from EC. The reaction solution contained 100 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 8.0) and 2% EC.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Purification of urethanase from C. parapsilosis
ce:section.ce:para: At first a HiTrap Q HP column and ÄKTAexplorer 10S system (GE Healthcare Bio-Science AB, Uppsala, Sweden) were used to purify urethanase. The active fraction was purified by repetition of the same procedure until one band on SDS–PAGE was verified. The N-terminal sequence of the purified protein was analyzed by the Procise 491 HT system (Applied Biosystems, Waltham, MA, USA). Blue native PAGE was performed to estimate the molecular mass of the purified protein with NativePAGE 4%–16% Bis–Tris Protein Gel and NativeMark Unstained Protein Standard (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) as a marker.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effects of temperature, pH, and ethanol concentrations on urethanase activity and stability
ce:section.ce:para: Urethanase activities at different temperatures (5°C–60°C) were measured in 100 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 8.0) for 2 h. Urethanase stability at different temperatures (5°C–60°C) were estimated by measuring the activity at 30°C in 100 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 8.0) after incubation at different temperatures for 18 h.

Urethanase activities at different pH values were measured in 100 mM sodium citrate buffer (pH 3.0–6.0), sodium phosphate buffer (pH 6.0–8.0), or bicine–NaOH buffer (pH 8–10) at 30°C for 2 h. Stability was estimated by measuring the activity at 30°C in 100 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 8.0) after incubation at 4°C in different pH buffers for 18 h. pH values before and after the reaction were directly confirmed by a glass electrode pH meter (LAQUAtwin, pH-11B, Horiba, Kyoto, Japan).

Urethanase activities in different ethanol concentrations (0%–30%) were measured in 100 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 8.0) for 2 h at 30°C. Stability was estimated by measuring the activity at 30°C in 100 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 8.0) after incubation at 4°C in each ethanol concentration for 18 h. All enzymatic activities were estimated with the mean and standard deviation of three independent assays.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of metal ion, NaCl, EDTA, detergent, and inhibitor on urethanase activity
ce:section.ce:para: For determining the effect of metal ions and EDTA on urethanase activity, enzyme assays were performed in the presence of various metal ions and EDTA at a final concentration of 10 mM in 100 mM McIlvaine buffer (pH 6.0). When we used sodium phosphate buffer, the precipitation occurred in a few ion solutions. Therefore, we used McIlvaine buffer in this study. To prepare metal ion solutions, CaCl2, MgSO4·7H2O, CuSO4·5H2O, FeSO4·7H2O, ZnCl2, and CoCl2·6H2O were used. Concentrations of NaCl, phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF), and Triton X-100 were 100 mM, 1 mM, and 0.02%, respectively. The urethanase activity was measured in 100 mM McIlvaine buffer (pH 6.0) for 2 h at 30°C. In the cases of Fe2+ and Co2+, the urethanase activity was assayed by measuring the amount of ethanol produced from urethane, because the Ammonia-Test-Wako kit could not be used in the presence of these ions.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Substrate specificity
ce:section.ce:para: Enzymatic activity toward EC, methyl carbamate, n-butyl carbamate, acetamide, propionamide, butyramide, and urea was assessed. The reaction solution contained 11.2 mM substrate and 100 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 8.0). Enzymatic activity was assayed by measuring the amount of NH3 produced from each substrate after 2 h at 30°C. One unit of hydrolysis activity was defined as the amount that released 1 μmol of NH3 from substrate per minute. The reaction schemes of urethanase and amidase are shown in Fig. S1.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Cloning of the urethanase gene and recombinant expression in S. cerevisiae
ce:section.ce:para: Urethanase gene was amplified by PCR using following two primers; 5′-TAGTTTCGACGGATCATGCTCACTGACAACTGGAA-3′ (primer-F) and 5′-CTAGGTCGACGGATCTCAATTTCTCAAAATGTTAG-3′ (primer-R). Genomic DNA from C. parapsilosis NBRC708 was used as template DNA. The amplified fragment was cloned into pG-1 vector using In-fusion cloning kit (Takara Bio, Shiga, Japan) and sequenced. S. cerevisiae YPH499 was transformed by the constructed plasmid. The transformant having the plasmid containing the urethanase gene was inoculated into 10 mL of YPD medium within L-shaped tubes at 30°C for 2 days. Then, it was inoculated into 500 mL of the same medium at 0.1 of initial OD660 in a 2 L baffled Erlenmeyer flask and cultured at 30°C with vigorous aeration in a shaker at 120 rpm for 2 days. Extraction of intracellular recombinant urethanase and purification method followed was same as that for native urethanase.

ce:section.ce:section-title: The accession number
ce:section.ce:para: The accession number of the cDNA sequence of CPUTNase is LC511748 in DDBJ.

ce:section.ce:section-title: RESULTS
Purification and molecular analysis of urethanase
ce:section.ce:para: The urethanase enzyme was produced and purified as described in the Materials and methods section. The urethanase was purified approximately 60-fold with an overall yield of 9% (Table S1). The specific activity of the purified enzyme was 4.2 U/mg. The purified enzyme showed a single band on SDS–PAGE gels (Fig. S2A). Its molecular mass was estimated to be 60 kDa. In blue native PAGE, the purified enzyme produced a single band at 240 kDa (Fig. S2B). Taken together, this suggested that this enzyme existed as a homotetramer.

The N-terminal sequence of this enzyme was MLTDNNKELA. This was analyzed against the online-accessible Candida protein sequence by BLAST, and sequence homology occurred with the hypothetical protein CPAR2_301880. This protein consists of 551 amino acids coding 1656 bases of ORF. The urethanase-encoding gene was amplified by PCR using genomic DNA from C. parapsilosis and cloned into a plasmid pG-1. Three different bases were found between the nucleotide sequence of ORF of CPAR2_301880 from C. parapsilosis CDC317 and that of this enzyme from C. parapsilosis NBRC708 (Fig. S3A). No amino acid differences were found in the protein sequences (Fig. S3B).

The constructed plasmid including cDNA of CPUTNase was transferred into a yeast, S. cerevisiae, for the expression of the recombinant CPUTNase. It was expressed as an intracellular enzyme, and the molecular mass of purified CPUTNase was estimated to be 60 kDa and 240 kDa by SDS–PAGE and blue native PAGE, respectively (Fig. S4).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of pH on activity and stability of urethanase
ce:section.ce:para: As shown Fig. 1 A, higher enzymatic activity was exhibited at higher pH values. Among the range of pH values used in this study, this enzyme had the highest activity at pH 10. Under acidic conditions (pH 3–5), this enzyme showed no activity. Stabilities at different pH values were estimated as residual activities after incubation at each pH for 18 h (Fig. 1B), and the residual activity was measured at pH 8. The pH of the reaction solutions was confirmed by pH meter, because enzyme solutions at different pH were added into substrate solution including 100 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 8.0). At pH values <5, this enzyme is unstable. The residual activity at pH 5.5 was almost half, and at pH values >6.7, the enzyme was stable.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of temperature on activity and stability of urethanase
ce:section.ce:para: We measured urethanase activity at 5°C–60°C. The optimum temperature of this enzyme was 43°C (Fig. 2 A). At 50°C, the enzyme activity was drastically decreased, and at temperatures exceeding 40°C, the enzyme was unstable. In this study, the stability of this enzyme was estimated as residual activity at different temperatures for 18 h. At 40°C for 18 h, enzymatic activity was lost (Fig. 2B). Because this enzyme showed the highest activity in the first 2 h after being added to the reaction solution at 43°C, denaturation might begin slowly at 40°C and become complete within 18 h.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of ethanol on activity and stability of urethanase
ce:section.ce:para: Activity in ethanol solutions is a property of this enzyme. Urethane is formed in ethanol solutions by the chemical reaction of ethanol and urea. Between 0% and 20% ethanol, more than 50% of the urethanase activity remained (Fig. 3 A). At concentrations <40% ethanol, the enzyme was stable (Fig. 3B). In 50% ethanol, this enzyme drastically lost its activity in 18 h.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of cations, chelator, and detergent
ce:section.ce:para: We tested the effect of several metal ions, EDTA, Triton X-100, and PMSF on the enzymatic activity of urethanase (Fig. 4 ). Zn2+, Fe2+, and PMSF strongly inhibited its enzymatic activity. Cu2+ and Co2+ also inhibited the activity, although more than 20% of the activity remained. Mg2+, NaCl, EDTA, and Triton X-100 did not significantly affect the activity.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Substrate specificity
ce:section.ce:para: Urethanase activity toward three kinds of carbamate esters were measured (Fig. 5 A). This enzyme showed the highest activity toward EC, 70% toward methyl carbamate, and 30% toward n-butyl carbamate.

Amidase activities toward four kinds of amide compounds were compared with each other (Fig. 5B). This enzyme showed almost the same activity toward acetamide, propionamide, butylamine, and acrylamide. Activities toward amide compounds were about 60 times higher than the enzymatic activity toward EC. This enzyme did not show activity toward l-ornithine, l-glutamic acid, l-glutamine, l-aspartic acid, l-asparagine, l-arginine, l-citrulline, or urea.

ce:section.ce:section-title: DISCUSSION
ce:section.ce:para: Until now, fewer than ten microbial urethanases had been purified and characterized. Only one fungal urethanase (from P. variabile JN-A525) had been studied, and its molecular mass was estimated to be 13.7 kDa; however, its sequence was not reported. In this study, we isolated a new urethanase from C. parapsilosis (CPUTNase) and identified its coding sequence (LC511748 in DDBJ). The molecular mass estimated by the predicted amino acid sequence was 61.7 kDa, which was almost same as the 60 kDa estimated by SDS–PAGE. The molecular size of CPUTNase was more than four times larger than the urethanase of P. variabile. In this study, recombinant CPUTNase was successfully expressed in S . cerevisiae. Because this recombinant CPUTNase showed the same traits as the native CPUTNase (Fig. S5), this identified nucleotide sequence was treated as the urethanase coding sequence.

CPUTNase was estimated to be a homotetramer consisting of four molecules of the 61.7 kDa protein. Until now, the molecular mass of only four urethanases were known. The urethanases of B. licheniformis and P. variabile were estimated to be a 160 kDa tetramer (42 kDa × 4) and a 96 kDa heptamer (13.7 kDa × 7), respectively. The urethanase of R. equi was estimated to be a monomer protein of 55 kDa. The urethanase from Citrobacter sp. was estimated to be a 500–600 kDa protein by gel filtration chromatography, with no further information about the protein composition or quaternary structure. These comparisons suggest that CPUTNase may be a different type of urethanase from previously reported urethanases.

Alignment analysis of the amino acid sequences of CPUTNase with the urethanase of R. equi, which is the only urethanase with a reported sequence to date, indicated low homology. However, both urethanases have a GGSS motif that is highly conserved in the amidase protein family (Fig. S3B). Based on the structural analysis of the amidase, Ser-cisSer-Lys catalytic triad was proposed (18). These residues are conserved in CPUTNase (Fig. S3B). These serine residues might be attacked by PMSF and CPUTNase had strongly been inhibited. Because EC has an amide bond and an ester bond, either or both bonds may be the target of the enzyme. The protein sequence of CPUTNase suggests that the amide bond in EC is the target of this enzyme. Substrate specificity also supports that CPUTNase is an amidase family protein because its activity toward amide compounds was higher than that toward carbamate esters. Whereas the urethanase of R. equi was shown previously to exhibit amidase and esterase activity (11), CPUTNase herein did not catalyze the hydrolysis of an ester compound (p-nitrophenyl butylate). Because we were specifically searching for a urethanase, it was unexpected that our purified enzyme showed any activity toward acrylamide, which is also classified in the same group 2A carcinogen as EC. However, the degradation of acrylamide would also be an attractive application of this enzyme.

In 20% ethanol solution, CPUTNase had 73% activity that was comparable to the activities (54%–82%) of urethanases from B. licheniformis, Micrococcus sp. and P. variabile. The thermal stability of CPUTNase seems to be slightly lower than those of other urethanases previously reported. This characteristic would not be a problem for an application in the alcohol industry because alcoholic beverages are usually processed below room temperature. On the other hand, CPUTNase had low activity under acidic pH conditions and exhibited its highest activity at pH 10, the highest pH value that was tested. This is a unique characteristic of CPUTNase. It was reported that the degradation of EC was catalyzed by some urethanases under acidic conditions, and those had an acidic optimum pH (4.0–6.0). Although pH values of most non-distilled liquors are acidic, the pH values of some distilled liquors are in the range of the pH in which CPUTNase is active. Improvement of the active pH range by protein engineering may become the goal of a future study with this enzyme since recombinant protein expression of CPUTNase was successfully performed in this study.

Recently it was shown that acid ureases could act as urethanases. Urethanase activities of three acid ureases have been reported (14–16). These bacterial ureases are complexes composed of three different protein units (UreA, UreB, and UreC). Recombinant expression (19), protein engineering (20), and immobilization (21) of bacterial ureases have been studied. Acid urease studies have opened up candidates of urethanase because these acid ureases are structurally different from previously reported urethanases or CPUTNase. Despite discoveries of urethanases and the accumulation of information on the enzymatic degradation of urethane, more studies are needed to fully understand urethanase.

Although further screening of microorganisms producing urethanase may lead to the identification of more effective enzymes, setting these screening conditions may be difficult because all reported urethanases to date have been intracellular enzymes. Our results suggest that yeast may be a candidate of a urethanase-producing microorganism. In addition, amidase may become a candidate for urethanase activity as acid urease is. Further studies of protein sequence analysis and enzymatic characterization of other urethanases will contribute to our understanding of urethanase and its applications.
